## @aimarket/esim-rails — the SDK and the seller node

Part of the eSIM operator kit. The package existing eSIM operators onboard with: the seller node AI agents buy from over x402, a neutral supplier interface with ready adapters (eSIM Access, Airalo, eSIM Go, and HTTP for your own system), signed webhooks for your CRM and billing, the `esim.*@v1` JSON Schemas and the conformance check `esim-rails check`. Reference: SDK · integrations · onboarding; setup of the whole kit: operator guide; calling it: agent guide.

Open rails for selling travel data eSIMs through an AIMarket hub. Anyone with a wholesale account runs a seller node; buyers — AI agents booking trips, apps, a storefront for travellers — find the cheapest plan across every connected seller and buy it with one x402 payment. The hub routes and takes its routing fee; the seller is the merchant (its prices, its VAT, its refunds).

Status: v0.1. The wholesale client, offers, pricing, the order flow and the seller node (free signed quote and status, the paid order behind x402) are written and tested. A live test order (2026-10-14) went through `fulfil`, `status` and `release` against eSIM Access: the cheapest plan ($0.30) was allocated in about 2.5 s, the same payment sent again found the same profile, a wrong status token was refused, and the cancelled profile's price returned to the balance.

## The three capabilities

Capability  | Price  | Input  | Answer
--- | --- | --- | ---
`esim.quote@v1`  | free  | `country` (ISO alpha-2), optional `min_gb`, `min_days`, `max_usd`, `limit`  | offers covering the country, cheapest first — regional and global plans that include it count
`esim.order@v1`  | the offer's price, x402 (USDC on Base)  | `offer_id`  | `activation_code` (the LPA string an eSIM is installed from), `qr_code_url`, `install_url`, `iccid`, `apn`, `expires`, `status_token`
`esim.status@v1`  | free  | `esim_tran_no`, `status_token`  | state, installed or not, data used and total, expiry — and the activation code again

An offer (`src/offers.js`) reads the same whichever wholesaler is behind it: `offer_id`, `name`, `coverage {kind, countries}`, `data_bytes`, `data_gb`, `days`, `speed`, `networks`, `top_up`, `unused_valid_days`, `price {usd, currency}`, `usd_per_gb`. The wholesale cost never leaves the node. Ask with `min_gb` and `min_days`: without them the cheapest offer is often a 0.1 GB plan.

`scripts/catalog.mjs` shows a seller what it would sell, read-only: balance, plan count, the shape of the supplier's fields, and the top offers for a few countries at its margin. The first live read (2026-10-14) found 1 728 fixed plans, all with a slug, all USD and days; e.g. France 1 GB / 7 days at $0.70 wholesale.

## What the order flow guarantees (`src/order.js`)

  * One payment, one profile. The wholesaler's `transactionId` is derived from the payment, and the supplier treats a repeated id as the same order: a retry after a lost answer cannot buy twice.
  * The activation code goes to the payer only. It is in the answer and nowhere else — not in the node's store (a test reads the file), not in logs, not in any receipt or feed. The payer gets a `status_token` (an HMAC of the profile number under the node's secret) to read the profile again.
  * Delivered, then settled. The node verifies the payment, orders, waits for the profile (the supplier allocated the test order's in 2.5 s; the node waits up to 45 s), and settles only after that. A refused order buys nothing; an allocation that is still running is reported and resumes on retry with the same payment; a payment that fails to settle cancels the profile, which the supplier refunds while it is unused.
  * The price is checked twice. The order carries the wholesale price the offer was quoted at, so a plan whose price changed since the quote is refused by the supplier rather than charged.

## Suppliers

  * eSIM Access (`src/esimaccess.js`): signed requests (`RT-AccessCode`, `RT-RequestID`, `RT-Timestamp`, `RT-Signature` = HMAC-SHA256 of timestamp + request id + access code + body under the secret key — the supplier's own test vector is in the tests), prices in 1/10 000 USD, 8 requests a second, no sandbox (a test order is cancelled and refunded). Keys are read from files and never logged, returned or sent anywhere but the supplier's host.
  * Next: eSIM Go, Airalo Partners — each is one more client behind the same offers and order flow.

## The node (`src/node.js`, `src/server.js`)

Route  | 
--- | ---
`POST /quote/invoke`, `POST /status/invoke`  | the hub's provider contract: `{success, result}` with an Ed25519 `X-Provider-Signature` over the request-bound canonical the hub verifies
`POST /order`  | `{offer_id}` — an unknown offer is a 400 before any price; then the x402 paywall (`src/paywall.js`: CDP facilitator, USDC on Base, the offer's price read from the request, paid to `PAY_TO`); the answer is released only after settlement
`GET /listing.json`  | the two hub listings and where the order is bought
`GET /healthz`  | catalogue loaded, provider key, whether orders are on

Configuration is in `src/server.js` (keys as files; the status secret and the provider key are made on first start). Without `PAY_TO` and `CDP_KEY_FILE` the node quotes but takes no orders.

## Connecting as a seller

The kit's `docker-compose.yml` runs this node behind Caddy at `https://<domain>/agents/`, beside the storefront and the federation node. The operator guide covers the wholesale account ($50 first top-up), the keys, the CDP key for x402, `node.toml` and the test order. `deploy.sh` is how modelmarket.dev runs its demo node (`DEMO_MODE=1`: quotes, no orders).

Selling to consumers makes you the merchant: in the EU that means VAT on telecom services in the buyer's country (OSS). The rails do not hold anyone's money.

## Test

    **One exact domain, registered for one year to the supplied registrant.** The quote shows the supplier cost, fixed markup and final amount before payment. For example, a $10 supplier cost plus a $2 markup gives a 12 USDC order; these are illustrative amounts, not a registrar tariff.
